<reason>A (CON) built the cleaner path to victory. From the opening, A framed harms as contingent policy choices and goods as structural, then turned B's own remedy—English retained as the working channel with reformed institutions—into the debate's decisive concession: if the ideal world keeps English dominant, the harms are not inherent to dominance. B's escape (channel dominance vs. evaluation hierarchy) was analytically sharp, especially the closing's "two rankings" distinction and the author/audience asymmetry, but it stayed asserted against A's network-gravity argument and required B to shift what "dominance" meant between speeches. B also honestly conceded it could not name one knowledge system destroyed specifically by English, leaving its harms mediated and partly speculative against A's concrete, present goods (one research conversation, safety protocols, MT pivot serving the smallest languages). A answered both pressure questions directly and substantively (network effects requiring standing; stock-vs-flow translation quality), while B's answer to A's Q2 was a concession plus threshold shift. Both were disciplined, well-structured, and rhetorically strong, but A made the debate easier to decide: fixable, policy-transmitted harms against structural connectivity goods, with the motion's net-harm burden unmet.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 concession trap (A2.1): B's remedy preserves English dominance and merely repairs institutions around it, converting the motion's target into a policy problem. B never fully escaped it—B4.1's channel/requirement distinction and B4.2's "rules are how dominance operates" were strong counters, but they conceded that the fix keeps English dominant as medium, which A pressed through every later speech.</best_rebuttal>
